projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Fred Luther Baker was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: This is Chris Simon interviewing Fred Baker in Moab, Utah, at his house on the 25th of May, 2004. Just a few things first. We're going to take the interview, starting out where you were before the war and then your experiences during the war, and how it has affected you afterwards. The very first thing we need you to do is have you state your name, what war and what branch of the service you were in.

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: My name is Fred Baker, and as we stated, the address is here in Moab. I was born in 1917, which would make me 86 now I guess. I've been in Moab now for twenty years, living in this location here for about seventeen years now.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Where were you born?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: I was born in Texas in Hill County, which is about 50 miles south of Ft. Worth, close to Hillsborough, which brings it down to the county seat of Hill County. I came to Tulsa, Oklahoma, with my parents when I was about a year old, and lived there through my younger grammar school years. My mother went to work as a medical assistant for doctors there in Tulsa, and eventually, my mother and father separated. My father went back to Texas and took up the farm that my grandfather had and stayed down there.

I subsequently went down to Texas to the farm on occasions and spent two or three years down there when I was around 8, 9, and 10 years old. Then back to Tulsa for junior high school and then over to Young Round College in Arkansas. This was a boarding school for three years of my high school years. I left there in 1933, went back to Texas and worked the farm down there for two years, then back to Tulsa, and then by that time, as you probably know, it was in the midst of the Depression and job were really at a standstill, nothing to be had, so I went into the Army at that time, when I was 18.

I spent two years in the Army, at Ft. Warren in Cheyenne, Wyoming, and decided that I wanted to get out, go back to school, so I left the Army then and went to Plainview, Texas, where my aunt had a court reporting school. I attended that for two years and went into the court reporting business, and went to Houston. This was a couple of years before WW II.

Of course I was exempt from the draft due to my Army service but as soon as WW II started, the draft immediately became effective for me, so I decided that I'd go over to the Navy and see what I could do before I was called up for the draft, so I went to the Navy office there in Houston and they happened to be looking for a court reporter for the courts martial and the wards of investigation work down in Corpus Christi, at the Naval Air station there.

They sent me down there and called the Naval Air Station legal office and confirmed that they were looking for someone in my business so that's how I wound up in the Navy then for the rest of my military career.

I spent about 18 months I guess, down at the Naval Air Station there at Corpus Christi in the legal office as a yeoman first class. As soon as I first arrived there and they found out that I'd had military training in the Army, they decided I didn't need to go through a boot camp. They just put me to work, so they sent me right over to the legal office without much ado there and I went right into my business there of reporting the courts martial and taking care of the business there at the legal office.

Then after about 18 months there, they had a system in the Navy then where a first class petty officer or above could be recommended by his commanding officer for a commission. My commanding officer said why didn't they recommend me and give it a try. I thought, well, I was a little dubious about the prospect there but I said okay, so I wound up then as an ensign after three or four months. I went on through my Navy career then as a commission officer rather than enlisted. From the Naval Air station there, they sent me to Patuxent River, to the Naval Air station in Patuxent River, Maryland.

I stayed there only about three or four months I guess, and then I received orders for the Pacific, and to report to San Francisco for transportation. That was my next move. I had a little car there and drove to San Francisco from Maryland, and went aboard ... it had been the SS America, which was a big luxury liner that the Navy took over for use as a carrier during the war, a transport carrier. I think there were 6000 men aboard that ship that went over to New Caledonia.

I got off there and went up to the New Hebrides, and up to Guadalcanal. I was assigned to a combat air transport unit up there which was the South Pacific Combat Air Transport and they abbreviated it to SCAT. Then I spent a year out there in that organization as an air transport officer. They would fly high priority supplies and passengers from the different stations out there where they had been cleared for an airstrip, cleared for landing, and that was our operation out there.

I had about three different islands that I was assigned to during my tour of duty with SCAT. It was a very interesting time in my life out there because I got to do quite a bit of traveling back and forth up through the islands. I would usually be assigned to a station where I had 12 or 14 men with me, and we operated the station or their weather operation. Is there anything you want to ...?

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Yeah, I'll pick up on a few. So what exactly were you doing, was it scheduling or ...

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: It was scheduling the planes for their trips up and down the islands there. For instance, Guadalcanal for awhile was our headquarters and we flew, starting down somewhere around New Caledonia on that area. Originally they went all the way to Australia, and back up through.

But as they cleared the island for operations, we went further south into the Pacific and then Guadalcanal eventually became a headquarters, and they had planes in flying on further up the line, Bougainville, Green Island, and then further down south to ... the islands further south. Then west up through ... well from the time they got to the Philippines, their service is pretty well finished out there. That was the type of work that they did at that time.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Did you come in after the Marines had already captured the islands and things were fairly stable or were you part of the combat troops?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: No, you have it right. The Marines or the Army would clear the island enough so that they could build an airstrip. The CBs came in, built airstrips, and there was enough activity there that the CBs had to carry their rifles with them on their bulldozers with them and so forth because they would be sniped at occasionally and on ... as they got an airstrip in, that was the basic thing that they needed and we started flying in and out of that particular island.

It was calm enough there that we didn't get into any actual combat operations. They were pretty stable from that standpoint. Our duties was to schedule flights out and some of them were evacuation, medical evacuation flights where they'd have some wounded men aboard with a flight nurse, and some of it was high priority materials that they needed up and down the line.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: What was a typical day like? You must have had some good friends there ...

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Oh yeah, especially in the CBs because what we would do would be to go into an island and attach our unit to a CB unit there for meals and so forth. So I got to know the CBs very well and they were a great bunch of people out there. They did all of the groundwork for putting in communication lines, building roads, and actually, they'd be just like a community out there by the time they got the airstrip and the roads and some of the Japanese prisoners would comment that they had no idea what had been done in those islands or they probably would have given up sooner if they had because they had a complete organized layout there, everything that was needed, water, supply, and things like that.
So I knew the CBs of course and got very well-acquainted with the men that worked with me and they were a varied crew there that you would have that worked with you.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Tell me about some of them.

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Well, for instance, we had a jockey in our bunch in Green Island, when I was there, and we considered him quite a little character. He would get into the medical chest and drink the alcohol out of it. We sort of calmed him down and said "Hey look, we needed that for medical supplies; don't be drinking up our alcohol." That was just an incident that I recall.

We were all very close because we had been out there for awhile. The object was to get our time in and get back to the States when we could. When we had a chance, we'd get a supply of beer from the CBs or something and have a little party some evening, you know, and cooking up some of the goat meat that we got from the Australians. That's part of our land lease program there, I guess, from the Aussies.

During my stay up at Green Island, the New Zealanders came in there, the New Zealand Army attachment, came in and assumed island command, they call it, which is to take over the island itself and the Aussies, the Australians also had a unit there. One of the men in the Australian Army was assigned to SCAT as sort of a liaison officer between our units. The CBs built me a hut where I lived next to the munitions dump close to the bluff overlooking the ocean there, and I had a second one built in case there was a second officer there so I told the Australian that if his commanding officer agreed to it, why not go ahead and take over that extra hut I had because they just slept in their tents and they had a little coke fire in front that they brewed their tea on and so forth.

It was pretty rough living. So he did and his commander agreed to it and he moved in there. So I got to know him quite well and we could swap our beer ration. Life was much easier having somebody to talk to. I still remember his name, Les Ridge, lived in Sydney, Australia and I thought some time I'd try to see if he's still around Sydney and try to locate him maybe.

That was one of the places that I'd set up at SCAT. The capital island of the New Hebrides at one time, and that was really sort of a jungle wonderland that you think of the Pacific; they call it the ideal Pacific setting. That came in that category. It had a lot of wild orange trees and avocado and everything just growing through the jungle.

The natives there had been to the mission school and were really quite well educated. The native population, and they lived out on a little island to themselves. For one reason, the mosquitoes wouldn't bother them out there because they were far enough out away from shore. I went to a wedding there one time of one of the persons out there and it was sort of an education to see how they lived and the way they kept their little huts and everything spruced up.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: What was the wedding like?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: It was quite an affair. It went on for about 24 hours, all night and part of the next day they danced and sang and had quite a celebration. It was a sister of the young fellow that came over and worked for us at our station there. You can have someone assigned to you from the native population and they would be paid for their work there by the government and they'd come over and just do things you wanted done around your quarters and everything.

This young fellow was about nineteen years old and his sister was the one that was getting married, so he invited me over to their wedding. It was, as I say, quite an education to go over and see a native wedding. I was there for several months. Each place I'd usually spend four or five months there. I got to know the young native boy that worked there well enough that he gave me an outrigger canoe that he wanted me to have for my own, so I had something additional to do there in my spare time, get out in my outrigger.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: So did you go out on the reefs and stuff?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: You can get out quite a ways, as far as their island and in between and the nurses there at the local Navy hospital, they're on the island, learned that I had an outrigger, so I had friends coming down to go out on the outrigger with me [laughs], so those are some of the things you can find to do outside of your routine.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: So it sounds like there was a regular South Pacific, like the musical, where you have the nurses and ... [laughs]

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Quite a bit the same. I mean they had the nurses of course they were very well protected up there. They kept them in their quarters, but you had a chance, you could make arrangements to take a nurse out on a little tour of the island or something and give them a chance to look around. You could get your jeep out and pick one up.

When I was down at New Russel Islands, at the Naval base there, we considered it quite civilized there because they had movies underneath the tarpaulin instead of sitting out in the rain watching the movies. We thought that was really living it up a bit. I made arrangements to pick up a couple of the nurses out there and I had a lunch fixed up and we went out on a picnic on the island so they could have a chance to see some of the rest of the country, which would be the only way they could get out to visit around a little bit.

The duty that I had was ideal for me because I was the only officer in my unit up there and down at our base there on the airstrip, it was nearing the daytime duty hours, but I had a jeep and could get around the island. It was about ... Green Island for instance was an atoll, about fourteen miles long, all the way around the atoll. There was a road, the CBs had built a road all the way around the island and there was a unit there. It was the Navy Patrol Boat operation, all to themselves there, and I was invited out once to a party out there, and they were a wild bunch [laughs] believe me.

You've probably heard stories about the PT-boat people ... they had a sign up above their little bar that says "To hell with the torpedoes, let's drink the alcohol" or something to that effect. You had occasion to run into all types and kinds of course. In the process, in the Efate Island, which is the capital island of the New Hebrides, they had a little town there and that's where the native population lived that I was talking about. They had a store there. They were carrying a lot of supplies. They were like sort of an English outpost.

Of course, all those islands originally were plantations. They were actually coconut plantations that they went in and built all this stuff among all the coconut trees. I was sort of the supplier there for our trips coming through Efate there, they depended on me to pick up the rum and drinks and the pilots coming through could take it up and take it on into their bases wherever. So I got to know quite a few of the pilots through my being the supply officer there.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Were these combat pilots or were they transport pilots?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Well, they were transport pilots. Of course, SCAT was a three dimensional organization. We had an Army, Marines and Navy combined. We had a Marine colonel, he was the officer in charge of SCAT and then we had some Army personnel that were assigned as ground personnel, and then we had both Marine and Army pilots. But they were flying the old C-47 or DC-3, which was so familiar back in those days; they were called the "workhorse of the Pacific." That was the term for it because it was just a durable old plane and that was the type of plane that they flew.

It wasn't equipped for flying passengers but we had some that would come in and crawl up on the stacks of mail that we had aboard [laughs] and just ride along with us. Because they didn't have any seats in them particularly, they just carried mail and high priority equipment and stuff on them. As far as that part of the Pacific, we finally ... another Navy fella that went out the same time I did to report to SCAT and we were assigned together in the Russels there because our time was coming up to be returned or get orders back to the United States. They paired us there at this SCAT station in the Russels [Solomon Islands].

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Where are the Russels?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: The Russel Islands, part of the chain there of the Pacific Islands that we were running up through. That was where the small naval base was located, in the Russel Islands. I actually had a naval captain that was a commanding officer. He and I were assigned together there to wait out our short time to get orders back to the States, we thought, but in the meantime, the order had come down that General MacArthur would assume command of that area of the Pacific out there, and General MacArthur wasn't one to rotate people back very quick.

[laughs] He had men that had been out there for three years I think. He changed the time from twelve months for personnel under his command to eighteen months, and we were close enough to the mortar of his command area that the Navy just shipped us over to the Russel Islands and we were eligible then to come back, but then the Navy did the same thing. They changed the rotation time from a year out to eighteen months [chuckles] so we were stuck anyway with the time limit.

The person that I was stationed there on at the Russel Islands with was Mark Berman, and I've often ... I don't know whether you're familiar with Chris Berman, the sports commentator that has a lot of, he's now with ESPN, I think and he used to be with CBS, but he looks enough like Mark that I often, I even tried to get in touch with him to find out if his father was Mark Berman because he looked a lot like him and he'd be the age to be his son, but I've never made that connection to find out.

Mark and I were eventually ordered back, at the end of twelve months anyway, and our time was expiring then in the South Pacific, and ordered back to Honolulu to the Naval air station there in Hawaii and went with Naval Air Transport Service there, and spent the next six months in the terrible duty of Hawaii [laughs] go to Waikiki Beach swimming, and sort of, actually, it was a little bit too civilized for us when we first got back there.

There were three of us came back from the islands together and we made it up to each other, "let's go in and put in for duty in the Philippines" and we went in there and they looked at us like they thought they ought to put a straitjacket on us for making such a suggestion as that, and they said "No, I don't think we're going to do that." So we went ahead and spent our time there, but we thought we were so used to the jungles out there in the Pacific and everything that we wanted to go back but we didn't do that.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: So what year was this? Was the war still on?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Yeah, right. As a matter of fact, I was still with the Naval Air Transport Service, and ordered back to the States, and this would have been probably '44 I guess, but it was right shortly after we got back to the States that VJ day happened. They signed the truce with Japan in the Pacific out there. That happened about that time, right after the incident of the bomb in Hiroshima, the atom bomb incident.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Do you remember hearing about that?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Oh yeah, we were all very aware of that. Of course it wasn't too long after that that they signed the treaty with Japan for peace. Then I went to Olathe, Kansas, which was headquarters at that time for Naval Air Transport Service, the naval air station there at Olathe, Kansas, right out of Kansas City a ways. Mark Berman and I spent, must have been, three weeks there, waiting for orders to get an assignment to a station and we had to report in each day out at the base out there but other than that we had nothing to do but report over to the swimming pool and go swimming [laughs] and back into Kansas City or something, so ... we were in Kansas City at the time of the big celebration of VJ Day and everything.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: What was that like?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Oh it was quite ... as a matter of fact, we went into Kansas City, and it was a huge celebration. You know, everybody was in the streets, and you remember the picture of the nurse being hugged by the sailor? It was a tremendous celebration going on there, for just about all night that night. Then after that, Berman and I thought we would be assigned to New York to the naval air station there in New York and we were already to go. We had wives with us, and we had a one seat roadster. The four of us would go back to New York in that. [laughs] I had fixed it up with a little rack in the back of the seat where somebody could sort of crawl in as a bunk back there and then riding three in the seat, but that didn't happen. Mark was ordered to New York and I was ordered to Phoenix, Arizona, to the Naval Air Transport Service there in Phoenix, out at Sky Harbor. I was there at Sky Harbor for three or four months in Phoenix, and received orders then for termination of my service with the Navy. I went back to Tennessee, I think, to be discharged there.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Did you want to be discharged?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: I was pretty happy actually in the service. I had a much easier time of it I think than a lot of them did. A lot of guys, of course, I never did have duty aboard ship. The only time I was aboard ship was on that big transport going out to New Caledonia. I was happy all the time I was with SCAT out there. I thought, I'm pretty happy to have the duty that I had. I thought at the time I would stay in the Reserve, go ahead and sign up, and I think the only reason I didn't is a lawyer friend of mine in Tucson where I ended up, he was out at the naval reserve station there in Tucson the night that we were supposed to either sign up or resign from the reserve, and he said "Oh, Fred, we're going to be too busy to be in the reserve," so I thought about it and I thought, "oh, I should stay in the reserve" and I always thought I made a mistake, but I didn't stay in the reserve after I got out, but I had four years then to my naval credit, which made me six years total of military time.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: That's a long time. I want to go back to Hawaii just because ... when did you get married? Were you married the whole time?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: I got married at Corpus Christi shortly after I went down there, married a girl from Tulsa, and we were married in Houston. We went up to Houston and were married there, so I was married through my service down in the Pacific and came back from Hawaii and we came into not San Francisco, but close to San Francisco, where we landed, and then my wife was down in Long Beach there in California and we joined there, got together and reported then up to Olathe, Kansas, to the duty there.

It wasn't exciting from the standpoint of any actual combat, the experience, because I think the closest we came to having anything happen to us there was one of the F4U fighter planes on Green Island, each morning they went on a little flight over to New Guinea and patrolled the coast over there for any Japanese ship activity in that area. They carried a 500 lb. bomb on each one that they'd drop over there somewhere and they, one of them coming back, they landed right over our quonset hut, right over our headquarters, coming flying back, and one of us, his bomb had stuck, and just as he had got over our abutment there, the thing came off and dropped right in our ... but it didn't have time to arm.

Each of those bombs has a little propeller arm on it and it has to know a certain length of time to protect the plane that it's been released from before it would go off, so it hit and bounded off across the abutment there and it wasn't more than six or eight feet off of the corner of our little weather hut. [laughs] As it happened, we had two weather men in there and they thought, "Boy, we had somebody watching over us there" because they were that close. But that's about as close as I came to getting hit by any armament of any kind.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: That's probably good.

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Yeah, you're pretty lucky if you can go through four years there and not be shot at or anything.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: One of the things that a lot of guys have talked about is going into the Army or Navy was their first chance to meet people that were really different from themselves, for instance, Mexicans or Jews or whatever. Did you find that?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Not too much. Actually though you find them from every part of the country of course. You get the Southerners with the southern accent, you know, and then from New York, and then from just about every place, but there's one thing you've got in common and that is your service that you're in and everybody becomes pretty much on a friendly basis through it all. It has a sort of cementing quality, the fact that you're all in there for the same reason, and you become friends with just about all of them. Out of all the people that you meet after you get out, there's only one person I ever ran into that was in SCAT out on the Pacific and that was down in Bisbee, Arizona, when I was down there for a couple of years. This one young fella down there that turned out he was in SCAT the same time I was that I knowingly ran into.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Did you keep in touch with any of the guys?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: No, I haven't and I thought I should have because Berman and I, Mark Berman and I, spending that much time there on the Russel Islands together, we became very close friends and I thought later I should have maintained contact with him because I often thought of him and his wife and mine were with us when we were in Kansas City or Olathe, we were all the four of us together. I was telling us about the arrangement we were going to have to ride in the little coupe. You meet a lot of people and you sort of expect and it actually is a little odd, all the accents that you run into.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: How did you keep in touch with your wife when you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Just through, in those days, mail was about the only way you had, and of course it would be slow, very slow sometimes three months or something before you got a stack of mail and you might get the whole package at one time. My mother sent me a fruitcake, I remember, that I received out there [laughs] I think, Berman and I were on the Russel Islands when I got that, and you find out nobody wants anything to do with fruitcake out in the Pacific, it's a little too hot for fruitcake. But mail was the only way that you had of reaching anyone and of course we didn't get a letter in the mail each time the mail came in. When I was in Honolulu at the Naval Air station there, I was the air transport officer, they call it, which was the same thing I was doing with SCAT, where you're running the weight and balance measurement on the planes before they leave to make sure they're in balance when you run the passengers. You're carrying a lot of passengers there so you're running the passenger list through to make sure that you have the right passenger, that you don't have a stowaway aboard. [laughs] Because there was a little indication that somebody might be stowing away wanting to get back to the States a little sooner, so you had to watch out for that. That was a type of duty you had on that and we ran 24-hour duty, so we'd run an eight-hour shift during the day one week, and maybe then swing shift the next, then midnight the next. It was changing times all the times on the shift. The plane that I came back I remember, FDR Jr. was on that flight. He came back on the same plane, the President's son.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: And was he in the service also?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: He was either in the service or a civilian attache I guess of some type, I don't remember whether he actually was in uniform or whether he was in some type of civilian service for sure. The planes back in those days, they switched over to the four engine DC-6s, they called them, which was a much bigger plane than the old C-47s, you know, but still flying one from the Pacific back to Honolulu was quite an experience because the seats on there were let down metal seats that you just sit on and let down on the side, and then folded up for freight and so forth when they needed, so you'd wind up laying down on the deck [laughs] stretched up rather than try and sit up in that aluminum seat there. I think it took something like eighteen hours I guess to make that flight. They had a station in Johnson Island, I don't know whether you're familiar with that part of the Pacific out there, but it's south of Hawaii and it's sort of a fuel stop for planes going in the Pacific. You make a stop there and another stop I think further out. There was the duty there in Honolulu there at the Naval air station was much more like it would be stateside. You wore your tie and shirt and everything, no more shorts and short-sleeved shirts that you wore out in the island. Little bit more spit and polish and the dress code and so forth.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Was that out at Eva or was it actually in Honolulu?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: The naval air station is right there in Honolulu, right there on the edge. What's the field where all the bombing went on, Pearl Harbor, and I guess it's Eckman Field out at the end, and they're joined by one runway, it came all the way through to the station there in Honolulu. The station itself though which was also the Honolulu International Airport, and that was operated off of it and we operated nearly all the traffic then. When I first went there they were flying the old China Clipper in. Do you remember the old 6-engine big flying bullet that they ran? Well, financially it was a dud. [laughs] The TWA tried to fly it for awhile but they only could do it with a subsidy from the government to keep it going. So the Navy took that over and flew that thing and it would only hold eight or ten passengers, and the rest of it they filled with mail, and the thing held a tremendous amount of mail, so that's pretty much what they used it for. I remember they had the little carts hooked together. They'd have about ten of them that they pulled up away from the thing and they'd have all of those would be filled up with mail, coming ashore from the old clipper. It was interesting to see it land out there because it would come across the bay there, with the big wake behind it, coming in.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Now what did you do on your time off? I know there was a big nightclub scene in Honolulu.

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Actually I never did go down ... I went swimming in Waikiki quite a bit and Honolulu at that time was a far cry from what it is today. The Moana Hotel, for instance, and the Royal Hawaiian were the only two hotels on Waikiki Beach over there, and today it's like Miami Beach in Florida. It's just a solid string of hotels and so forth, but then, the Royal Hawaiian Hotel had been taken over by the navy submarine crews. That was their R and R place there in Honolulu, the Royal Hawaiian, and the Moana was pretty much all military. There was no tourist activity of course at that time.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: How did you hear that the war had ended? Were you out on the streets or was there an announcement?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Well, of course, it just came over the radio every place, and then they had the big celebration in Kansas City, and we happened to be there, so we were well aware of what was going on there. I'm sure that word spread pretty rapidly every place. The only ones that didn't get it were some of the Japanese that were isolated back in those jungles and I understood some of them three years later were still out there and didn't know the war had ended. They were living with the natives and just didn't know that they had an end to the war until somebody came through and announced it to them much later, but they, of course everybody in the service knew it through the radio.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: How did you feel?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Oh, everyone was very, very elated over it. It was, after four years or better than four years I guess then, it was something to really celebrate. People, some of them, like some of the Australians, they had been out since they had gone over to Europe and had been in operations over there, it was a long time since they had been home and they were looking forward to it when they got back to places like Green Island where we were not too far from there getting home then. But there were some of them that had been out a long time, looking forward to returning home so they were even more jubilant about the end of if than we were.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: They were more endangered too. The Japanese were going to be invading Australia.

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: They were into, what is the country next to that I just mentioned, New Guinea, that's where the bombers off the Green were hitting the Japanese in New Guinea so they were working their way and of course long about that time they changed tactics, General MacArthur's idea was that they'd get by, but they found out they could do much better by just isolating the Japanese troops who were on one side of an island and patrolling the shore there and keeping any supplies away from there and skip on to the next island and they just shortened the war, I would say, by half anyway, by getting away from having to clear an island completely before going on to the next island.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: When you think about that period of your life, was it a good time or a bad time?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Oh, it was a good time. I mean, of course age-wise you're optimistic about things anyway, and I was still only twenty-eight or so when I got out of the Navy so I still had things to look forward to. I thought I'd like to change my occupation from being a court report to, I was always more into livestock and animals and outdoors and that type of thing, but as fate would have it, I channeled right back into court reporting again and first thing I knew I was back in that business with court report in Tucson, where I wound up after I left Phoenix, and came up to Tucson. He had me helping him out on jobs. Then I got the official reporter for court down in Bisbee, Arizona, and I was there two years, then the opening came up in the federal court in Tucson, and then I came up to Tucson and was there thirty-six years in Tucson. It just happened I ended up in the same field that I had been in when I first went into the Navy.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Did you have trouble adjusting to civilian life?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Not a great deal. You start getting busy and first thing you know, you are back to where you were before you ever left, so I didn't have a great deal, not like it would be for a guy that was out there in a Marine unit or something, really being shot at everyday. I wasn't having to recover from shell shock or anything. I just went back to it.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Would you go back to the South Pacific if you had a chance?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: Yeah, as a matter of fact, I've often thought I'd like to go back to some of the places. Of course, they have that memorial at Guadalcanal that was set up in commemoration of the battles at Guadalcanal, and it would be interesting to see that and I missed my chance to go to Australia when Berman and I were there at the Russels, my rotation for leave came up for a thirty day stay to go down to Australia and I always wanted to go and Mark talked me out of that, he said, "you go down there and your orders are going to come in, they'd go back to the States, and they ain't going to sent them back if you're down there." So I thought, well, I don't want that to happen, so I turned down my chance to go down to Sydney for thirty days. I even had a letter from my friend Les Ridge, he wrote to his wife and said "see that Fred gets to see Sydney and some of the sights around Sydney and introduced me to her" so I had an in there, I sort of had a guide lined up, but I didn't make it. New Zealand would be a place I'd like to go and see.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: Looking back now, how do you feel about WW II? Was it a good thing to have fought?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: WW II was inevitable. There wasn't any chance we were going to get out of it after the attack on Pearl Harbor. We were just in it then and no chance to go anyplace else and we were just about in it anyway. I mean, you know, through our help to Britain and our allies over there, it was just a matter of time the United States would have been in the middle of WW II anyway. So that was sort of the precipitating cause there at Pearl Harbor. It was a unique situation in that civilians during that war were just as much into the war as the guys that were in uniform. I mean they had rationing and people joined together and got into the bomber plants and got jobs there and went to work as riveters, Rosie the Riveter, and whatnot, so it was a thing that everybody was just faced up to being in the war and went at it. That's the only thing that won it for us; we were really unprepared for war when we started that with Japan. The United States was ... it was only about three or four years before that that I was in the Army and they had 60,000 men in the United States Army, if you can believe that, just four years before, so they had to build from that to several hundred thousand to go into combat in WW II plus all the motorized equipment. At the time I went in, the Army, they had horse-drawn artillery were still operating, mule-drawn howitzers and so forth. Nobody went by truck or anything. It was all walking infantry that got you where you were going, so it ... when I look back on it, it was really a time of amazement for me to see that, how it could be turned around in the time that they had to do it. They didn't have any of the ... the fighter planes that they had when they started out were no match for the Japanese zero. It wasn't long until they were passing them up and flying planes that the Japanese couldn't keep up with and couldn't catch. They were surpassing them. Japanese realized that, long before the end of the war there, that things were really going by them. If the Japanese, of course in those days, supply lines were limited where they could go across the Pacific or anything. But if the Japanese had only known, they could have gone from Pearl Harbor right on into San Francisco bay there in very short order. There was no preparation to keep them out. The only thing that saved that was the distance then. They didn't have planes that could fly that distance. We were sorely unprepared but within a year's time things were really humming in the United States toward getting war underway.

sp.speaker: Chris Simon
sp.p: I just have a minute or two left. Is there anything else that you want to say?

sp.speaker: Fred Luther Baker
sp.p: I could go on for ... [laughs] no that's fine. That pretty well covers the length of my military time as far as that goes. My Army time was sort of a unusual circumstances then and, as I say, you were taking care of your mule on machine gun carts, for instance, were towed behind them on the mule team and of course all the heavy artillery was horse-drawn. We went up to Pole Mountain reservation in the summer for manure up there, and actually that was a pretty nice time up there. You just go up there and build a permanent camp up there for the summer and I was amazed that about the first morning up there seeing the milk trucks from Cheyenne come lumbering down the road there into the camp and delivering milk from Cheyenne to our camp, so it wasn't a time of privation or anything. Beautiful country up there, it's north of Cheyenne, Wyoming. I remember it snowed up there the first of August. We had a pretty good snow up there. As far as any hardship that I had in the Navy, I always considered myself pretty lucky even out in the Pacific. We'd sit on a coconut log to watch a movie, but other than that there wasn't any real hardships to speak of. The CBs saw to oh, I can tell you about the little set up there on Green Island, the CBs had built the hut, I think I told you about it. It had bookshelves in it, and fixed a bed with strips of inner tube so that you had a soft bed and then they built me a shower. Out there you depended on rainwater; catching rainwater on Green Island because the atoll was narrow enough that if you drilled a well in the center, you'd still get the salt water, so they build a little casement on a platform out there, put a little ... [recording ends]
